Ask SEOGBTools support to confirm what your plan includes and whether any usage caps apply.

Indexification is marketed as a URL submission service. Before considering any service, check the page you want people to find. Open the preferred URL in a browser, confirm that it returns the intended content, and look for redirects, duplicate versions, or a noindex directive. Google decides whether a page belongs in its index.

Make pages easy to discover

Link to a new product from a relevant category and include the canonical URL in your sitemap. For pages you own, open Google Search Console and inspect representative URLs. If the report points to an alternate canonical, compare the declared canonical, internal links, and sitemap entry.

Track changes by page type

Keep a small log with the URL, publication date, inspection status, and any fix you made. Compare affected categories or templates when a problem repeats. If several products share nearly identical text, improve what each page offers before requesting another crawl. For related tooling, browse the SEOGBTools catalog.

Diagnose an indexing problem before submitting URLs

Take one affected page and inspect the exact address in Search Console. Check the Google-selected canonical and compare it with the URL in your navigation and sitemap. If the page redirects, inspect the destination. If the preferred page is accessible but excluded, review whether a closely related page already answers the same question. Write down one change you can test and when you made it. Treat Indexification as a separate third-party service. Its submission records cannot establish whether Google indexed a URL, and a submission cannot guarantee inclusion or a ranking.

Start by identifying the kind of indexing problem

When a page does not appear in Google, first decide what you need to check. The page may be new and waiting to be discovered. Google may know about it but have chosen a different URL as the canonical version. The page may also be indexed already and simply rank too far down for the phrase you searched. Each situation calls for different work. Submitting the same URL again gives you little insight into which issue you have.

For a page you own, open the exact URL in Google Search Console and read the URL Inspection result. Record the address you entered, the date you checked it, and the status Google reports. Compare that record with the page you intended to publish. If your store uses both old and new product slugs, verify that you are inspecting the current version and that the old one leads visitors to the right destination.

If the page is indexed, review its search performance. A new category may receive impressions for specific product phrases before it appears for the broad phrase you had in mind. Check the queries and average position for the page. If Google rarely shows it for relevant searches, improving the page's focus or helping readers discover it through related categories may be more useful than sending another submission.

Clean the URL list before checking it

Start with a list from your sitemap, catalog export, or publishing log. Remove repeated rows and group addresses that refer to the same content. Your spreadsheet might include a product's clean URL, a version with tracking parameters, and an old slug that redirects. Keep the variants as notes if they help you diagnose a problem. Use the preferred live URL for the inspection itself.

A small shop might start with five pages that matter to customers, such as the home page, a category page, and three updated products. A larger site can select a sample from each important template. If all three products from one category have the same problem, check other pages that share that layout or publishing process before trying to repair individual URLs.

Use one row per preferred page. Include the page type, when it went live, where it is linked, whether it is in the sitemap, and what Search Console reported. Add a column for the next action. Clear notes such as “replace old category link with preferred product URL” are easier to act on than a general note that says “indexing problem.”

Check the page as a visitor

Open the preferred address and look at what loads. Make sure you can see the main heading, description, and useful page content without signing in. Check the final URL if the browser redirects. A product may appear to work when you open it from an admin preview but be unavailable at the public address. Use a public browser view to confirm what ordinary visitors see.

Check the response and the page's indexing directives with the tools you already use. If the public page returns an error, fix that first. If the page intentionally has a noindex directive, confirm whether that matches your publishing plan before removing it. A staging copy or a duplicate filter page may have no reason to appear in search. Removing a directive without understanding the purpose of the URL can expose pages you meant to keep out of search.

In Search Console, the live test can help you see whether Google can currently access the page. The live result and the recorded index status answer different questions. A live test describes the page Google can fetch at the time you run it. The index status describes Google's recorded information about that URL. Compare them when you have just fixed a redirect, changed the page, or removed an accidental noindex directive.

Make canonical signals consistent

A canonical URL is the preferred version of a page when several addresses display substantially the same content. A store might use a clean product URL in its catalog and add tracking tags to campaign links. If those addresses show the same product, check that the clean address is the one you use in the sitemap, category links, and canonical declaration.

If Search Console reports a different canonical, inspect both addresses and ask why Google might see them as duplicates. A product page and a category page should usually serve different purposes. If a variation page is almost identical to its parent product, decide whether customers need it as a separate searchable page. Keep a note of the desired result so you can tell whether a change helped later.

Avoid changing multiple signals without a record. If you update a canonical declaration, switch the sitemap entry, and rewrite internal links on the same day, document what changed and why. When a later crawl picks a preferred URL, you can check whether the whole site now points to that version. If the wrong page is still selected, the notes give you somewhere concrete to start.

Use internal links and sitemaps for discovery

A useful internal link gives visitors a reason to move from one page to another. A category page can link directly to its active products. A product guide can link to the corresponding catalog page when the reader needs availability or pricing. Check that the destination is the preferred address and that the link text makes sense to someone who has never seen the site before.

Review pages that can only be reached through the sitemap or a search box. A useful product can be difficult to find if the category never links to it. Add a link from a page that already serves the relevant audience. A footwear size guide can point to the shoes it discusses, while a general homepage link may give readers too little context.

Include canonical pages you want Google to discover in the sitemap. When you replace a URL, check that the sitemap reflects the public page you intend people to visit. A sitemap helps communicate the addresses on your site. Google may still choose whether and when to crawl or index them. For Google's own guidance, see how to request a recrawl.

Choose a submission method that fits the job

For a few pages you own, URL Inspection gives you a direct way to review each address and request indexing where the option is available. For a larger group of new or updated pages, check the sitemap and make sure the pages are linked from relevant areas of the site. The method you choose should fit the number of URLs and your ability to verify the result later.

Indexification is a third-party service. If you are comparing access, verify the current terms and what its reports actually show. A submission or processed status inside a third-party tool describes work in that service. Use Search Console on the property you control to confirm Google's indexing status. If you do not own the site that hosts a link, ask the publisher about the page or rely on the public evidence you can verify.

Keep the decision simple. If the page cannot load, fix access. If Google sees several copies, check which version the site points to. If the page is discoverable and technically ready, give Google time to crawl it and review whether the page provides a reason to appear in search. Repeated requests for the same address do not accelerate Google's processing.

Run a sample check before scaling

Suppose you publish twenty products in a new category. Start by opening the category and selecting three products. Pick one simple product, one with variations, and one that replaced an older listing. Confirm each page can be found from the category, returns the right content, and appears under the desired URL in the sitemap. Write down where the examples differ.

If the simple product works and all variation pages show the same canonical issue, inspect the shared variation template. If the replaced listing redirects to the home page, check whether it should instead point to the corresponding product. If none of the new pages is linked from the category, fix the category first and review another sample before spending time on individual requests.

Keep the original inspection and the follow-up record together. For example, note that you changed category links on Monday, requested a recrawl for one product on Tuesday, and checked the recorded index status again later. This makes it easier to spot which changes are associated with improvement. It also helps you avoid concluding that one unrelated change fixed the entire group.

Compare Indexification access with your actual needs

Before ordering any service, decide what you expect it to do. You may need to discover technical problems, keep a record of submissions, or measure whether important pages are getting search traffic. These are separate jobs. Search Console can help you inspect Google's view of pages you own. A crawler can help you find redirects and missing links across many pages. A submission service has to be evaluated against its documented features and current terms.

Compare practical limits such as how many addresses you need to work with, whether you can export your records, and what happens when access ends. Start with a small set of representative URLs. If the service does not give you the evidence you need to make a decision, keep using the checks that do. For related research on the content itself, see KWFinder for keyword research.

Frequently asked questions

Does submitting a URL guarantee Google will index it? Google decides whether to include a page in search. A submission is a request. Use URL Inspection to check what Google reports about your page.

How long should I wait after asking Google to crawl a page? Google says crawling can take from several days to a few weeks. Check the page's status later and keep working on any problems you can verify while you wait. Google's recrawl guidance.

Should I submit URLs with tracking parameters? Use the preferred version in the sitemap and for normal inspection. Review a parameterized version when you need to diagnose how it behaves or why Google selected it.

Can Search Console check a page on a site I do not own? URL Inspection is for URLs in a property you can access. If a third-party page is important to your work, ask its publisher to check it or use the public information available to you.

What is the first thing to check when a new product is missing? Open the public URL, confirm the page loads, and inspect it in Search Console. Check whether the page is linked from the catalog and whether the sitemap lists the preferred address. The first inspection usually tells you what to investigate next.

How do I report progress to a client? Show the sample size, the pages checked, the issues you found, and the changes you made. Include the date of the next review. Keep indexing status separate from impressions and clicks so the client can see whether pages were discovered and whether they later attracted relevant search traffic.
